newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Close result seen in Friday's Irish election.
newsitem.headline: Close result seen in Friday's Irish election.

text.p: Ireland holds elections on Friday to choose between the centre-left coalition of Prime Minister John Bruton and a rival centre-right alliance under Bertie Ahern which has led opinion polls from the start.

The last poll before voting starts showed Ahern's Fianna Fail (FF) and its smaller Progressive Democrats (PD) ally nine points ahead of Bruton's two-and-a-half-year-old "rainbow coalition" of his own Fine Gael, the Labour Party and Democratic left.

But the survey, in Thursday's Irish Independent newspaper, showed that as many as 14 per cent of the 2.7 million electorate remained undecided, a variable which reinforced forecasts that the result could be inconclusive and create a hung parliament.

Many voters were reported to have waited until a Wednesday night televised debate between Bruton and Ahern before making up their minds on whether to follow the prime minister's urging to "stick with the rainbow" or dump it.
Bookmakers gave Bruton unchanged odds of 7/4 on remaining prime minister or taoiseach while Ahern's odds were shortened to 1/3 from 2/5.

Victory for Ahern would buck the recent trend in France and Britain and install a right of centre government committed to hold down government spending, crack down on crime with a policy of zero tolerance and slash 11-percent unemployment.

It would end the term of a previously untried alliance of Bruton's Christian Democrat Fine Gael and its left-wing allies which has presided over an era of unparalleled prosperity, earning the economy the title "Celtic Tiger."
The Irish Times said Bruton gave "the best performance of his political life" in the Wednesday night debate, confounding critics who said he lacked warmth, charisma and spontaneity.

He appealed to voters to ignore history and return an incumbent government for the first time in almost 30 years by giving his coalition the 85 seats it seeks to control parliament. It has the same number in the previous assembly.

Bruton also ignored Ahern's taunts of having increased government spending by eight per cent, twice its target: "I have no apology to make to any economist for spending money to improve education," he said.

Ahern repeated campaign promises to bring down the top rate of tax from 48 to 43 per cent over five years but Bruton said his plan would only benefit middle class wage earners, not people on or below the poverty line.

Both are committed to Ireland being among the first wave of countries to join economic and monetary union (EMU) but Ahern's ally, PD leader Mary Harney, has voiced concern that Ireland should wait until its main trading partner, Britain, joins.
"The one thing you cannot have in a coalition government is doubt about currency policy," Bruton said.
"The Progressive Democrats say we should be very careful about our competitive position if Britain does not enter, that's all," said Ahern. "We will have to watch our fiscal position."

The two rivals share the same goals of fostering a settlement to the Northern Ireland conflict, where 3,200 people have been killed in 28 years, and reducing unemployment, which has dropped two points to 11 percent in the past two years,

They are also promising to end a crime wave which broke into the national conscience with the unsolved murder of investigative reporter Veronica Guerin last year. She was thought to have been killed on the orders of a drugs baron.
